conflicts.point: Whether traditional negligence standards and pre-deployment audits can effectively verify safety for foundation models characterized by non-linear scaling and rapid weight updates.

positions.stance: Supports negligence standards paired with mandatory pre-deployment audits and runtime telemetry, arguing they successfully catch systemic failures without paralyzing innovation.
Argues that negligence standards and pre-market audits fail because non-linear scaling and rapid internal weight changes make pre-deployment verification impossible.

conflicts.point: Whether the legal burden for high-risk system failures should fall primarily on upstream foundation model developers via strict liability or on downstream commercial deployers through targeted tort enforcement and contract oversight.

positions.stance: Prefers bounded downstream liability and targeted negligence rules to protect open-source development and accelerate beneficial medical and economic applications.
Demands strict liability for upstream developers to internalize irreducible risks and prevent developers from externalizing harm onto the public.

verdicts.conflict: Whether traditional negligence standards and pre-deployment audits can effectively verify safety for foundation models characterized by non-linear scaling and rapid weight updates.
verdicts.rationale: Both camps lack definitive longitudinal data from commercial deployments at scale. Accelerationists point to existing software auditing precedents, while safetyists cite the unpredictable behavior of non-linear neural networks. Neither side has demonstrated through empirical testing that their preferred standard reliably prevents catastrophic failures while maintaining deployment velocity.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Longitudinal audit data comparing safety failure rates between foundation models deployed under negligence rules versus those governed by strict liability.

verdicts.conflict: Whether the legal burden for high-risk system failures should fall primarily on upstream foundation model developers via strict liability or on downstream commercial deployers through targeted tort enforcement and contract oversight.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic position citing FTC Section 5 enforcement offers a concrete, tested mechanism that avoids the economic disruption of strict liability. Accelerationists and safetyists debate theoretical risk internalisation, but the skeptic position maps directly onto existing regulatory powers used by federal agencies. This makes the negligence and consumer protection approach significantly more politically feasible and legally coherent.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Judicial rulings or statutory failures showing that current consumer protection statutes cannot reach systemic harms caused by upstream foundation models.
